text:
I quit my job at Intuit in October last year with eleven thousand dollars in savings and a Trello board with four cards on it. The plan was to build invoicing software for freelance electricians and plumbers, the kind of people who still send PDFs through email and use QuickBooks like a filing cabinet, not a tool. I called it Fernwood, because the domain was six dollars and everything else was taken.

The first three months were mostly cold calls. I talked to forty-two contractors, took notes in a Google Doc, and built nothing. By January I had a prototype: contractors could photograph a handwritten invoice and it would auto-fill client, hours, and rate from a job history. Nobody asked for that feature. What they actually wanted was for payments to show up faster, so I ripped out the OCR work in February and wired up Stripe instead. That decision alone probably saved the company.

We signed our first paying customer in March, a plumber in Tacoma named Russ who found us through a Reddit thread and paid forty dollars a month without ever getting on a call. By August we had thirty-one customers and eleven hundred dollars in monthly recurring revenue, which sounds small because it is small. I did the math in a spreadsheet on my kitchen table more times than I'd like to admit, usually around midnight, usually landing on the same answer: not enough, not yet.

In April I pushed a database migration at 11pm on a Tuesday and double-billed nine customers before I noticed, around 7am, from an angry email. I refunded everyone by hand before breakfast and wrote a Stripe webhook test I should have written in February. Nobody canceled over it, which surprised me more than the bug did.

My cofounder left in June. He'd taken a job offer from a company that could actually pay him a salary, which was the right call for him and a genuine setback for us. I don't think I've fully forgiven the timing, even though I understand the reasoning. We haven't talked much since.

I'm writing this in September with about four months of runway left. Fernwood has thirty-one customers, a support inbox I answer myself, and a pricing page I've rewritten nine times. Russ in Tacoma is still paying his forty dollars a month. I don't know yet if that's enough to build a company on.

I started Bramble a year ago last week, in the spare bedroom of my apartment, with $41,000 in savings and a conviction that turned out to be half right. I thought restaurant managers wanted another scheduling dashboard. What they actually wanted, I learned after four months of cold calls and diner coffee, was to stop calling seventeen people every time a line cook phoned in sick. So we built the sick-call feature first and backed into the rest of the product around it.

The first six months were mostly rejection. I pitched forty-three restaurant groups in Ohio and Michigan and closed three. One owner, in Toledo, told me my demo looked like it was built by someone who had never worked a dinner rush, which was true, and which I still think about. We signed our first paying customer in March — a four-location pizza chain in Dayton, $180 a month — and I remember checking the Stripe dashboard four times that day like it might change its mind.

Money was the constant problem underneath every other problem. I paid myself nothing for the first nine months and my co-founder, Priya, paid herself just enough to cover her half of rent. We lost our second engineer in August, three weeks after a client's schedule failed to sync on a Friday night and forty employees got no shift notifications. He left for a company with a 401k match and I don't blame him. I spent that whole weekend on the phone with angry restaurant owners, apologizing, and Priya rewrote the sync logic from scratch by Monday.

By December we had nineteen customers and had stopped losing money on each one, which is a lower bar than it sounds like but felt enormous at the time. We still haven't fixed the onboarding flow, which takes new customers an average of eleven days when it should take two. I keep meaning to prioritize it and keep not prioritizing it, because something else is always on fire.

I don't know yet whether Bramble becomes a real company or a good story I tell at parties. The Dayton account is still with us. The Toledo owner who insulted my demo signed up six months later, after a competitor's product crashed during his Saturday rush. I try not to read too much into that. Mostly I'm just tired, and mostly it was worth it, and I'm not sure those two things resolve into anything cleaner than that.

I started TNX a year ago last week, in a spare bedroom with a laptop and eleven thousand dollars from my own savings account. I'd spent four years doing IT for a hospital system and watched front-desk staff fight the same scheduling software every day — it was built for dentists in 2011 and never updated for anyone else. That was the whole pitch, really: fix the double-booking, and everything else can wait. The first six months were mostly me writing code and emailing people who never wrote back.

We built a scheduling tool for physical therapy clinics — not exciting, but the market has almost no software written for it after 2015. Our first customer was a clinic in Rochester that agreed to pay $200 a month if we fixed their double-booking problem. It took us three weeks longer than I promised. I remember apologizing to the office manager, Denise, on a Tuesday call, and she just said "everyone's late, honey" and hung up.

By March we had eleven clinics paying us, which sounds better than it was — total revenue was $2,300 a month, less than my rent. My cofounder Raj left in April. He didn't storm out; he sat me down at a diner and said he needed a paycheck his wife could count on, and I couldn't argue with that. I hired his replacement in June, a contractor named Priya who worked twenty hours a week and somehow shipped more than Raj had full-time. She's the one who talked me out of building a mobile app that quarter, which in hindsight was the best product decision either of us made all year.

The low point was probably July, when our biggest customer canceled after a billing bug double-charged forty patients. I spent two days on the phone reversing charges and eating the Stripe fees myself. I still don't fully understand what caused that bug — we patched around it rather than root-causing it, and it hasn't happened again, but I'd be lying if I said I know why.

We ended the year at thirty-one clinics and $9,400 in monthly revenue. Not a hockey stick. Enough to pay Priya and keep the lights on, barely.

I don't know if this company works yet. Some days I think the market's too small and we should pivot toward billing software instead of scheduling. Other days a clinic manager emails to say the tool saved her front desk an hour a day, and that's enough to keep going another month.

Looking back at year one—we launched with three people, a demo that worked maybe sixty percent of the time, and enough runway to feel brave for about four months. Almost none of what I expected to be hard was actually hard, and almost everything that broke us, I hadn't thought to worry about.

The product itself came together fast. We had something customers could touch within six weeks. What nearly killed us was everything downstream of "it works": billing edge cases nobody tested, a support queue that turned into a second full-time job overnight, a contract with our first enterprise customer that took longer to negotiate than the product took to build. I'd budgeted for engineering risk and gotten blindsided by operational risk instead.

The low point came around month seven. We lost our second engineer, our biggest prospective customer went quiet for six weeks and then said no, and I remember sitting in a coffee shop doing the math on payroll and coming up eleven days short. I didn't tell my cofounder how close it was until later—which I now think was the wrong call. The fix was embarrassingly obvious: I called five people I'd been too proud to ask for help, and one of them wrote a check. Pride is expensive.

What actually saved the year wasn't a growth hack or a pivot, it was narrowing. We started the year trying to serve three kinds of customers and ended it serving one, the one that was already paying us and asking for more. Every week we spent chasing the other two was a week we weren't compounding on the segment that wanted us. I wish I'd made that call in month two instead of month eight.

I also learned I was a worse manager than I thought. I hired people I liked instead of people the stage needed, and I held onto a hire too long because letting them go felt like admitting I'd been wrong. Both mistakes cost us months.

Twelve months in, we're small, profitable in a fragile way, and still here—which was not guaranteed in month seven. I don't think the lesson is "it gets easier." It doesn't, particularly. The lesson is that most of what breaks you in year one is boring and unglamorous, and the people who make it through aren't the ones with the best idea. They're the ones willing to ask for help before they're out of runway instead of after.

We incorporated Fenwick Labs in March, and by May I'd already burned through the buffer I told my co-founder Priya would last a year. I remember the exact number: $34,000, gone in ten weeks, mostly on a contractor who built us a dashboard nobody used.

The idea was simple enough — inventory reconciliation for small furniture retailers, the kind of shop that still runs on a spreadsheet and a guy named Dave who's been there since 1998. We thought we'd sell to Dave's boss. Instead we spent four months learning that Dave was the actual decision-maker, and Dave did not want software that made his spreadsheet obsolete. That lesson cost us our first two customers, both of whom churned within a month.

By August we had eleven paying accounts and a product that mostly worked, except for a sync bug with Square that would silently drop transactions over $500. We didn't catch it for six weeks. One customer, a rug importer in Tulsa, found out when her books were off by $4,200 and called us, understandably furious. I still think about that call more than I think about our first sale.

Hiring was the part I was least prepared for. I brought on our first engineer, Marcus, in June, and I had no idea how to manage someone — I'd never managed anyone. I gave him vague direction and then got frustrated when the result didn't match what I hadn't actually said. He left in October, not angrily, just tired of guessing. That one's still on me.

What kept it alive wasn't a pivot or a breakthrough. It was Priya's stubbornness, mostly, and the fact that three of our early customers kept renewing even after the Square incident, seemingly out of loyalty rather than satisfaction with the product itself — which is a strange thing to build a company on, but there it is.

We ended the year at nineteen customers, roughly break-even on hosting costs, and nowhere near a salary for either of us. I wouldn't say I have it figured out. I still don't know if Dave-the-inventory-guy is our customer or our obstacle, and a year in, I've stopped assuming the answer is fixed.

We launched Voltframe in March last year with four people, one enterprise customer we'd promised a demo we hadn't built yet, and $180,000 in a friends-and-family round that felt enormous until payroll hit in June.

The first three months went to that demo. We shipped it nine days late, and the customer signed anyway, mostly because their incumbent vendor had just had an outage. I thought that was a lesson about timing. It wasn't — the next two customers took four months each, and one of them ghosted us after a final call that I thought went well.

By August we had six people and no idea what our churn number actually was, because our billing system logged cancellations as "paused" by default. I found this out from a customer's Slack message, not from our own dashboard. We fixed the logging in an afternoon and spent the following week arguing about whether the real churn rate — 11% monthly, not the 4% we'd told our angel investors — meant the product was wrong or the sales process was wrong. We never fully resolved that argument. I still don't know which one it was, probably some of both, and one of our early advisors still thinks it was neither.

Money got tight in October. I cut my own salary to zero for six weeks, which sounds like a sacrifice in retrospect and mostly just meant I was annoyed at grocery stores. We laid off one engineer in November, our best one, because his part of the roadmap had shrunk. That's the part of the year I think about most, more than the product decisions.

Things turned in January, not because of a strategic pivot but because a customer's competitor asked to switch to us after a bad renewal conversation elsewhere. That one deal, $84,000 a year, put us over the line where the December numbers stopped scaring me. I wish I could say we earned it through a better sales process. We didn't; we got lucky exactly when we needed it.

We ended the year at fourteen employees, $1.4 million in ARR, and a churn number I finally trust. I would not describe the year as fun. I'd describe it as the year I learned our billing system lies by default, and that the people who leave are sometimes the ones you'll miss most, not the ones who were struggling.
